questions.q: Out of the box, how does the Kubernetes scheduler see a node with 8 physical GPUs attached?
options: Identically to a node with 0 GPUs — Kubernetes has no native concept of a GPU
As a node with 8 extra CPU cores
As a node that automatically gets nvidia.com/gpu capacity without any additional setup
As a node that must be manually excluded from scheduling
questions.explain: Kubernetes' built-in resource model only understands CPU and memory. Without a device plugin, GPUs are invisible to the scheduler regardless of how many are physically attached.

questions.q: What does the NVIDIA device plugin do once deployed as a DaemonSet?
options: It installs the NVIDIA driver on every node automatically
It discovers the physical GPUs on each node and reports them to the kubelet as the nvidia.com/gpu extended resource
It enables Multi-Instance GPU partitioning by default
It replaces the Kubernetes scheduler with a GPU-aware scheduler
questions.explain: The device plugin's job is discovery and advertisement: it finds the GPUs on its node and reports them as the nvidia.com/gpu extended resource so the scheduler can account for them. It assumes the driver and Container Toolkit are already installed.

questions.q: In a pod spec, how must nvidia.com/gpu be requested?
options: Only under resources.requests, never resources.limits
As a fractional value such as 0.5, by default
Under resources.limits, with requests and limits required to be equal
As a separate top-level gpuCount field on the pod spec
questions.explain: nvidia.com/gpu is only meaningful as a limits entry, and requests/limits must match — there's no built-in way to request less than a full GPU and get a fractional limit.

questions.q: What is the real purpose of combining a node taint on GPU nodes with a nodeSelector on GPU pods?
options: The taint is purely cosmetic and has no scheduling effect
The nodeSelector alone is sufficient; the taint is optional in every cluster
Taints only apply to control-plane nodes, never worker nodes with GPUs
The taint keeps non-GPU pods off GPU nodes, while the selector pulls GPU pods onto them — the two need each other
questions.explain: A nodeSelector alone pulls the right pods toward GPU nodes but doesn't stop an unrelated pod from landing there too. The taint is what actively excludes pods without a matching toleration, protecting expensive GPU capacity.

questions.q: By default, how many physical GPUs does a pod requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 receive?
options: Shared access to all GPUs on the node
Exclusive use of one entire physical GPU
One MIG instance automatically
A time-sliced tenth of one GPU
questions.explain: By default, nvidia.com/gpu is allocated as a whole integer — a pod requesting 1 gets exclusive use of one entire physical GPU, never a fraction, unless additional sharing mechanisms are configured (covered in the next lesson).
